reporting-org.narrative: Action Canada for Sexual Health and Rights

title.narrative: Sexual Rights Initiative (2021-2026)

description.narrative:
1. Build a strong intersectional feminist knowledge base and analysis with feminist thinkers-advocates from academic and research institutions, CSOs and movements, and use these ideas to advance and defend SRHR norms and standards.
2. Build the individual and collective power of feminist and SRHR advocates, particularly from the Global South, to (re)claim UN human rights spaces for accountability and justice.
3. Shore up support for SRHR by expanding our engagement with a wider set of states, particularly focusing on silent, undecided or states with ambivalent positions on SRHR.
4. Continue to improve our ways of working to better align with our intersectional, feminist, decolonial politics .

The Sexual Rights Initiative (SRI) is a feminist coalition of national and regional organizations from each UN region that come together to advance an intersectional feminist approach to sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) throughout the UN human rights system.

title.narrative: 4. State accountability to SRHR rights norms and standards

description.narrative: Advocates, CSOs and movements work individually and collectively to effectively hold states accountable to SRHR rights norms and standards using the international HR system.

title.narrative: Number of UPR submissions annually

description.narrative: 4.1 - Number of UPR submissions annually

comment.narrative: 15 stakeholder submissions were prepared for: UPR 47: Albania, Bhutan, DRC, Ethiopia (2), Costa Rica (3), Nicaragua UPR 48: Angola, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bolivia UPR 49: Armenia, Kenya and Sweden

Africa – 8 submissions Asia Pacific – 4 submissions EEG – 1 submission GRULAC – 2 submissions WEOG – 1 submission Themes: Women’s rights, SRHR, abortion, CSE, GBV, HIV, SOGIE, sex work, COVID-19, rights of marginalised persons. 24 collaborating organisations

Lower number of submissions aligns with SRI’s commitment to do fewer reports to enable us to prioritise quality and duration of support to national level partners. This indicator should be reduced for future years.
Total of 9 stakeholder submissions for the following countries: 50th Session: Malawi (2), USA (2), Panama (2) 51st Session: Nepal 52nd Session: Namibia, Paraguay

title.narrative: Number of Treaty Monitoring Body shadow reports annually

description.narrative: 4.2 Number of TMB shadow reports

comment.narrative: 5 TMB submissions Africa – 1 submission GRULAC – 4 submissions Themes: SRHR, abortion, CSE, GBV, HIV, forced sterilisation, COVID-19, rights of marginalised persons. 18 collaborating organisations

The advocacy advisor role dedicated to treaty bodies was revised to include HRC work, increasing SRI’s capacity to engage in HRC. SRI’s work on treaty bodies has been limited to prioritise work on norms and standards setting through GRs and GCs and supporting other organisations work on treaty bodies who are not Geneva based (such as IWRAW-AP’s CEDAW work)

description.narrative: 4.3 - Number of oral statements delivered during HRC sessions

comment.narrative: 41 oral statements including: 6 statements ID with special procedures 10 statements during GDs and panels 12 UPR adoption statements 13 joint statements Issues addressed: COVID-19, SRHR, abortion, CSO space and participation, racism, poverty and economic injustice.

42 oral statements were delivered 31 were joint statements 12 were made during UPR adoptions 17 were made during interactive dialogues with special procedures The balance of statements was made during panels or general debates.
Themes: SRHR and racism, colonialism, capitalism, abortion access, health systems, sexuality, gender, gender architecture, access and participation of civil society and human rights defenders.

title.narrative: 2. Feminist and advocate engagement in the human rights system

description.narrative: Feminist and SRHR advocates working on diverse and neglected SRHR concerns have the advocacy capacity (knowledge, skills and tools) to effectively engage in the international human rights system.

title.narrative: Number of feminist and SRHR advocates and CSOs attending SRI workshops and trainings

description.narrative: 2.1 - Number of feminist and SRHR advocates and CSOs attending SRI workshops and trainings

comment.narrative: 106 feminist and SRHR activists including 5-day intensive training sessions for the trade union delegation, intensive orientation, training sessions with members of the HRC 59 sex worker delegation, workshops delivered to three cohorts of advocates participating in CEDAW country reviews, a workshop delivered to women human rights defenders participating in HRC 59 and orientation sessions for SRHR advocates participating in HRC 60.
247 people attended 18 workshops/training

258 persons attended 16 workshops/trainings This translates into an increase of 4.45% from 2023 and 24.64% from 2022 results.
220 or 85% of the participants are from and working in the Global South compared with 78% in 2023.
International human rights advocacy, gender, sexuality, disability, SRHR, sex work, and economic justice are the main themes addressed in the workshops and trainings.
In 2021, 147 persons attended 7 workshops and trainings.

title.narrative: 6. Advances in UN human rights mechanisms

description.narrative: UN human rights mechanisms make substantive advances on SRHR norms and standards.

title.narrative: Number of recommendations made and noted that undermine SRHR during UPR sessions

description.narrative: 6.2b - Number of recommendations made and noted that undermine SRHR during UPR sessions

comment.narrative: The high acceptance rate of harmful UPR recommendations suggests that these recommendations are being made based on an assessment of the likelihood of the SuR accepting it, perhaps as a way to give support to the SuR for an existing harmful position. In this instance, there is little that can be done in the context of the UPR to get these states to note these recommendations but rather points to a much longer term approach that involves national and global advocacy.
49 recommendations with harmful content were made during the 44th, 45th and 46th sessions. Of these, only 5 harmful recommendations were noted.

description.narrative: 6.3 - Number of concluding observations, general comments (GCs) and general recommendations (GRs) that advance SRHR norms and standards from treaty monitoring bodies

comment.narrative: 157 SRHR recommendations were made by treaty bodies as part of country reviews. Incomplete data.
CEDAW Draft GR on Gender Stereotyping is a strong draft and will be critical to pushback against essentialist and gender binary trends emerging within the Human Rights Council.
Incomplete data but CERD GR on the Right to Health presents significant gains in SRHR norms and standards.

title.narrative: Number of reports, recommendations, statements and press releases by Special Procedures (SPs) that advance SRHR norms and standards

description.narrative: 6.4 - Number of reports, recommendations, statements and press releases by Special Procedures (SPs) that advance SRHR norms and standards

comment.narrative: 10 SRHR related thematic reports 200 SRHR recommendations in thematic reports 300 SRHR recommendations in country visit reports
12 thematic reports 76 recommendations from (non-SRHR) thematic reports 84 country visit recommendations 12 press releases* (incomplete data)

3 reports that the SRI contributed to and were cited demonstrated substantive advancement of SRHR norms and standards including: SP on Right to Development report on nexus between gender equality and the right to development (e.g. (d) Take effective measures to safeguard the sexual and reproductive health and rights of girls and women, including access to relevant services); WG on DAWG guidance document on substantive equality (e.g. para 68 on women’s autonomy with regards to sexual health and reproductive decision making); SP on racism report on intersectionality from a racial justice perspective (e.g (b) Improve the accessibility of policy, legal and other decision-making spaces through the provision of any necessary reasonable accommodations and by addressing any barriers to access faced by those with experiences of intersectional discrimination)

8+ recommendations Incomplete data but examples of positive SRHR recommendations made by SPs include: WG on DAWG’s and SR on Health’s separate guidance notes on sex work SR on Cultural Right’s report on sport SR on Poverty and SR on Housing’s report on homelessness and poverty WG on DAWG’s vision setting report SR on Health’s report on harm reduction
